study.title: Psalm 100 - Completion of the good and faithful God
study.overview: This psalm calls the whole earth to worship the LORD with joy, recognition and gratitude. The answer of faith is not cold or just individual: it involves voice, service, public worship, and memory of God's actions. The center of the psalm is that the LORD is God, made his people, care for him as a shepherd, and remains good, merciful and faithful from generation to generation.

outline.title: Universal Invitation to Praise
outline.explanation: The psalm begins with a strong call that all the earth exults before the LORD. Worship is presented as a joyful service, with song and disposition of the heart, not as mere outward obligation.

outline.title: To recognize who God is and who we are
outline.explanation: The basis of praise is the knowledge that the LORD is God and that it is he who made his people. The worshippers are compared to sheep of their pasture, and this leads to a grateful and public entrance in their presence.

outline.title: The final reason: kindness, mercy and fidelity
outline.explanation: The psalm shuts up showing why this praise is permanent: the Lord is good, his goodness endures forever and his faithfulness goes through generations.

study.context: The notes highlight that this psalm calls the nations to praise the Lord and, in the language of public worship, speaks of gates and courtyards connected to the temple in Jerusalem. Matthew Henry understands that the call extends beyond Israel and reaches the gospel community; Adam Clarke notes that the psalm was used in worship and associated with thanksgiving. The scenario, therefore, is of public and community worship, with gratitude for the mercies of God.
study.theology: Theologically, the psalm teaches that worship is born of who God is, not only of what we receive from him. He is sovereign, Creator and Pastor; therefore, the people are not defined by himself, but by divine election and care. Joy in worship is not mere enthusiasm, but a proper response to the constant goodness of the Lord. The text also states that God's mercy and faithfulness are not episodic: they support the history of his people from generation to generation. Thus, praise is universal, but at the same time deeply personal and pactual.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm summons all nations to come to worship the LORD and to recognize his goodness to Israel.
The call to praise God extends to all the lands and, in his reading, points to the gospel community, not just to Israel.
The "ports" and the "pathians" indicate public worship; enter them with gratitude expresses appreciation for the privilege of worshiping God.

questions: Is my worship of God marked by real joy, or just by religious routine?
I recognize that I am part of God's people because he made me his, and not on his own merit?
Have I entered into the presence of God with conscious gratitude for his goodness and faithfulness?
study.practice: Separate a moment today to transform the reading of this psalm into prayer: thank God for his goodness, confess that he is his Shepherd and praise him in a concrete way, with words and with a joyful attitude. If you participate in Christian worship or meeting, enter with the purpose of serving the Lord with gratitude, rather than just assisting. Throughout the week, daily remember evidence of God's faithfulness and use it as a reason for praise.
study.uncertainty: The notes do not inform with absolute certainty the exact historical context of the composition, nor do they allow to define in an indisputable way if the psalm was written for a specific occasion of thanksgiving. There is also an observation by Adam Clarke about the Hebrew title that involves a possible liturgical nuance of "offerta of confession," but this should be treated as interpretation, not as an undeniable fact of the text.
